sentences.text: Isla is fifteen now and Cnoc Dubh has six houses in it and a tarmac road that is cleared by a machine from Ardmore, usually within a day.
Her great-grandmother died in the March after the project.
The storm came on the eleventh of December and it was not a 1953 storm and nobody has pretended otherwise.
It was a bad one.
The road went, the power went for nine hours, and the school in Ardmore was shut for three days, and the whole thing was on the regional news for about ninety seconds.
Isla went out on the second morning to see to the hens.
It was flat white and there was no wind at all, which is the thing that happens after, and the ridge above the hollow was a clean grey line against a sky the colour of a plate.
She stood in the yard with the feed bucket and looked up at the scoop.

She looked for a long time — long enough that her hands went, long enough that her mother came to the door and asked her what on earth she was doing — and she did not see anything at all, and she went in.
She has thought about this a great deal.
If it was there, she could not have seen it.
That is not a get-out; that is the entire, well-documented, un-mysterious biology of the animal.
Isla has sat four metres from a ptarmigan on a bare ridge in daylight and been unable to find it while being told exactly where to look.

So the honest position, and the one she has settled on, is that she does not know whether there was a bird on the ridge above her house on the twelfth of December, and that there is no available method by which she could have found out, and that this is not a failure of the investigation.
It is what the animal is.
What she does know is that the machine from Ardmore came on the fourteenth and that everybody was fine.
She goes out and looks anyway, every time, and she is aware that this is not evidence of anything.

Her mother thinks it is a habit picked up from an old woman and is gently amused by it, and Isla lets her think that, because the alternative is a conversation she does not want to have on a doorstep in the cold.
She has been up to the scoop once in summer, in July, when they are brown and much easier.
There is a hollow in the peat up there about the size of a dinner plate, in the lee of a stone, worn smooth, facing directly down the glen at the fourteen — now six — chimneys of Cnoc Dubh.
She did not measure it.
She sat beside it for a while and then went down.
